The rapidities have added, and the speed for that added rapidity is on the flat part of the curve, below 1. Stack as many boosts as you like and it stays below 1.

Black is the charge's velocity: where it is heading, and how fast. The dotted circle grows as fast as light spreads out from the start, so nothing should ever get outside it.

4hfp12p6l27j8tn91lgqbeo42n.value: From here on, speeds are measured against the speed of light: 1 means as fast as light, 0.5 means half as fast. Light goes about 300,000 km a second, so even 0.01 is very fast, and a real train is at about 0.0000001.

4muua6j18n4m0b6gk9gs69vddo.value: Here the electric field (E) points up the screen, and the magnetic field (B) points straight out of the screen, towards you. The charge starts at rest. E gets it moving upwards. As soon as it moves, B pushes it sideways, which bends it round to the right and then back down until it stops, and then E starts it off again, a little further to the right. The path is a row of loops that drifts to the right.

5m0uvm3nj4bejq811c2frg371u.value: The same idea as in Part 1. In the spacetime algebra, the electric and magnetic fields together are a single object, and that object turns the charge's motion a little at every moment. When B is stronger than E the turn is an ordinary rotation, so the charge goes round in loops. When E is stronger the turn is a boost, so the charge keeps speeding up, the way Part 1's boosts did, and like them it never reaches the speed of light. When the two are equal it is a turn in between.

6gaogvump3442ns9hu00srdgle.value: Ordinary turns are easy to combine: turning by 30° and then by 40° is a turn by 70°. Boosts combine the same way, except that what adds up is not the speed but a number called its rapidity. For slow things, rapidity and speed are nearly the same number. For fast things they part ways: the speed is tanh of the rapidity, a curve that rises steeply at first and then flattens out just under 1.

7ad7dv3ddcg6d14sejcf0c271s.value: Try E = 0.4 and B = 1 first: the two charges make the same loops, because neither gets very fast, though the program's falls a little behind, since even at these speeds a moving charge is a little harder to turn. Then E = 1.2: Newton's charge speeds past light and leaves the circle, but keeps looping, while the program's charge runs off to the right and stays inside.

7p270e0ofb1hg63ikhhru3fsa9.value: E is at least as strong as B. Newton's charge still loops, since the magnetic push grows with its speed and keeps bending it back, but it drifts at E/B, at or past the speed of light, so it leaves the dotted circle. The program's charge stops looping and runs away to the right, faster and faster, but never past light: it stays inside the circle.

ata33ul90du29cpo3c4j3gt8c5.value: Credits: the spacetime algebra, with boosts as rotors, the spacetime split into relative vectors σₖ = γₖγ₀, the field as one bivector F = E + IB and a charge's motion as u turned by e^(dτF/2), is David Hestenes' (Space-Time Algebra, 1966; New Foundations for Classical Mechanics, 1986), as presented by Chris Doran and Anthony Lasenby (Geometric Algebra for Physicists, 2003) (prior art). Relativistic velocity addition is Einstein's (1905), rapidity as the quantity that adds is Robb's (1911), the force on a charge is Lorentz's, and the transformed fields are Lorentz's and Einstein's (prior art); here they come out of the rotor product rather than being written in. The page, its pictures and its words are ours.

dagqb6b81mlnh04vg05an6p04q.value: Relativity keeps the same two pushes: the same E, and the same sideways push growing with speed. What changes is how the charge responds to a push. Near the speed of light, pushing hardly changes its speed any more, so it gets harder and harder to turn. When B is stronger than E, the charge still gets bent back, but more slowly, so its loops stretch. When E is at least as strong as B, the magnetic push can never turn it round in time: E keeps pushing it on, and it runs off, closer and closer to light speed but never past it. So the running away is the relativistic effect, and the neat loops are Newton's.

heukkbm3be4veamav1g46qco7c.value: You might expect that once Newton's charge goes faster than light, nothing would hold it back and it would fly off. Watch the purple arrow. The magnetic push grows with the charge's speed: twice as fast, twice the push. And it is always sideways, so it bends the charge round without speeding it up. The faster Newton's charge goes, the harder it gets bent back. It speeds up while it goes with E, gets bent round, slows down while it comes back against E, stops, and starts again. As long as there is any magnetic field at all, Newton's charge loops, however strong E is.

ner491e3opec537g0bs6389h7k.value: The algebra is Cl(1, 3), the spacetime algebra: four directions γ₀ (time) and γ₁, γ₂, γ₃ (space), with γ₀² = 1 and γₖ² = −1. A multivector has 16 parts. The speed of light is 1.

pduhkaajfpiinq6lcortq1nfrl.value: Part 1. The boost by speed β along x is the rotor R = e^(φ/2 σ₁), with σ₁ = γ₁γ₀ and rapidity φ = artanh β. Since σ₁² = +1, the exponential gives cosh and sinh: a boost is a hyperbolic rotation. Two boosts multiply to R₂R₁ = e^((φ₁ + φ₂)/2 σ₁), and the ball's four-velocity is R₂R₁ γ₀ (R₂R₁)~, whose γ₁ part over its γ₀ part is tanh(φ₁ + φ₂) = (β₁ + β₂)/(1 + β₁β₂).

pskf3foq6b42ui788p8n0invso.value: Part 2. The field is one bivector, F = E + I B, with I = γ₀γ₁γ₂γ₃. The charge's four-velocity obeys du/dτ = F · u, and over a step dτ it turns as u → R u R̃ with R = e^(dτ F/2) (Hestenes). F² = E² − B² + 2I E·B: when F² < 0 the step rotor is a rotation, when F² > 0 a boost, and when F² = 0 it is 1 + dτF/2. Here E and B are at right angles, so F² is a number and clifford exp makes the rotor in closed form, with cos and sin or cosh and sinh. For fields at other angles the prelude has clifford exp by series.
